title: Resilient Transmission of Highly Structured Light via Active Convolved Illumination
summary: Wave propagation through lossy and noisy systems as well as spatiotemporally dynamic random media often limits the complex information that can be reliably transmitted or retrieved. Progress in adaptive optics, wavefront shaping, machine learning, and wave propagation theories has significantly advanced physical and computational correction techniques. However, many approaches remain constrained by restrictive operating conditions, limiting their ability to meet growing application-specific demands, such as higher spatial resolution in imaging and greater data capacity in communications, particularly in highly dynamic environments. Recently, active convolved illumination (ACI) was proposed as a novel framework for preserving the spatial structure of optical modes during propagation through strongly distorting environments, such as atmospheric turbulence. ACI aims to bypass the prohibitive complexity of global distortion tracking by combining spectrally localized characterization with compensation using a correlated auxiliary source. Here, we provide a comprehensive review of ACI, detailing the formulation of correlation-injecting and auxiliary sources and the role of segmented reciprocal-space characterization and distortion compensation. We explore extensions in free-space optical communication and potential high-precision phase measurement, and numerically evaluate interferometric strategies for experimental implementation. This work highlights ACI as a potentially versatile framework for distortion-resilient light transmission, with broad interdisciplinary utility ranging from atmospheric physics and remote sensing to telecommunications, target tracking, and biomedical diagnosis, offering flexible deployment either as a standalone paradigm or hybridized with existing optical systems.

title: 1.56 THz Full-Field Rydberg-Atom Imaging with 0.3 mm-scale Spatial Response
summary: THz imaging via Rydberg-atom up-conversion offers a powerful full-field modality with high sensitivity and rapid acquisition. However sub-millimeter imaging above 1 THz is still constrained by source power and beam-delivery loss. In this paper, we demonstrate a \(50~\mathrm{mm} \times 50~\mathrm{mm}\) full-field imaging at 1.56~THz by implementing the \(11P_{3/2} \rightarrow 10D_{5/2}\) transition of a cesium Rydberg-atom vapor. The measured spatial response FWHMs are \(0.314~\mathrm{mm}\) in horizontal and \(0.354~\mathrm{mm}\) in vertical for a \(0.5~\mathrm{mm}\) pinhole, alongside a sensitivity of \(31.7~\mathrm{fW}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1/2}/(6.5 \times 6.5)~μ\mathrm{m}^{2}\), and a frame rate up to \(300~\mathrm{fps}\). Under matched illumination, relay, and image-processing conditions, mask imaging at 1.56 THz reproduces finer features and edges with substantially higher edge contrast, deeper intensity-trough separation in line profiles, and recovered detail that remains blurred or unresolved at 0.55 THz. Furthermore, preliminary imaging of a \(200~μ\mathrm{m}\) tissue slice suggests morphological correspondence with H\&E histology histology, offered as a proof-of-concept for label-free tissue characterization. By validating the wavelength-dependent resolution scaling in Rydberg THz imaging, this work establishes frequency scaling as a general design principle for sub-millimeter Rydberg-THz imaging.

title: Deep, label-free, volumetric lifetime microscopy via low-noise, single pulse sampling
summary: Fluorescence lifetime imaging (FLIM) provides label-free metabolic contrast, but conventional time-correlated single-photon counting requires thousands of excitation pulses per pixel to avoid pile-up distortion, limiting imaging speed and increasing motion artifacts and photodamage. Here, we develop single-pulse analog sampling that combines sub-photoelectron read noise with a jitter-immune, frequency-domain estimator for accurate lifetime measurement at low photon counts. Single low-flux traces achieve a photon economy of $F < 1.5$ at 100--150 detected photons, enabling accurate lifetime estimation from a single excitation pulse in label-free, volumetric samples. In in vivo zebrafish eyes, single-shot acquisition recovered the lifetime content of 20-pulse averaging at one-twentieth the exposure, resolving endogenous lipofuscin heterogeneity. In intact mouse kidney, scattering and reduced photon throughput impaired lifetime contrast; this was mitigated by lightweight denoisers that enabled label-free lifetime imaging to 200 micron depth at one pulse per pixel. These results establish single-shot FLIM as a route to deeper, faster, motion-tolerant, low-photodamage lifetime imaging.

title: An Inverse-Designed Multilayer Selective Emitter for High-Efficiency Thermophotovoltaics
summary: High thermophotovoltaic (TPV) conversion efficiencies have typically relied on photovoltaic cells that reflect sub-bandgap radiation back toward the emitter. Here, we numerically investigate an alternative approach in which spectral selectivity is engineered primarily on the emitter side. We optimize an emitter consisting of 16-layer aperiodic MgO/Si coating on tungsten, for coupling to a GaSb cell with an antireflection coating and an Au mirror. A detailed-balance framework incorporates polarization- and angle-resolved emissivity, multiple reflections, and Auger nonradiative recombination. At an emitter temperature of 1500 K, the optimized structure suppresses 97.1% of the incident-blackbody-equivalent sub-bandgap power at the source; a further 1.9% is returned to the emitter by the cell, leaving 1.0% absorbed parasitically in the cell. The resulting modeled radiative-to-electrical conversion efficiency reaches 47.0%, compared with 30.8% for a SiC emitter paired with the same cell, while maintaining a comparable maximum electrical power density. These findings indicate that emitter-side spectral engineering could substantially relax cell-side photon-recycling requirements and provide significant improvement in TPV conversion.

title: Accessible 3D Printed Archimedes System for Accurate and Precise Density Measurements and Uncertainty Analysis
summary: Accurate and precise density measurements are important for characterizing solid materials and for evaluating physical properties that are strongly affected by porosity. While several methods are available for determining density, measurements of small or irregularly shaped samples can be limited by sample geometry, balance precision, liquid density, and other experimental sources of uncertainty. In this study, an accessible Archimedes density measurement system was developed using 3D printed components and an analytical balance for the measurement of solid and liquid densities. The measurement of solid densities requires knowing the exact density of the liquid. Therefore, copper, vanadium, and indium standards were used to measure the densities of ethanol (0.8116 +/- 0.0005 g/cm3), distilled water (0.9982 +/- 0.0013 g/cm3), and hexanes (0.6748 +/- 0.0016 g/cm3), all of them showing strong agreement with literature values. Uncertainty analysis indicates that the relative uncertainty in the measured solid density decreases with increasing sample mass and balance precision, while higher density liquids can further reduce the required sample mass. The uncertainty of the immersed mass measurement was found to have a greater influence on the calculated density than the uncertainty of the air mass measurement. An open-source Archimedes LS software was developed to analyse liquid and solid densities including the corresponding uncertainties. These findings demonstrate that an accessible 3D printed Archimedes system combined with an open-source software provides a practical approach for improving the consistency and comparability of density measurements between laboratories.

title: A thorough review on Deep Learning approaches to 2D-to-3D Registration in Medical Imaging
summary: 2D-to-3D image registration is a key component for several medical imaging purposes such as intraoperative guidance, enabling the alignment between preoperative 3D volumes and real-time 2D images. While conventional optimisation-based methods often struggle with non-convex objectives, sensitivity to initialisation, and high computational demands, deep learning (DL) has emerged as a promising alternative, offering improved alignment robustness and the potential for real-time performance. This review provides a comprehensive analysis of DL frameworks developed to address the challenges inherent in 2D-to-3D registration. We first outline how core concepts of DL are adapted to the registration problem. We then examine recent methodological advancements from multiple perspectives, including pipeline design, architectural innovations, and domain adaptation strategies. Particular attention is given to quantitative metrics, highlighting how performance is defined and measured across studies. Across the 41 included studies, we find that direct regression is the most common pipeline (23 studies, against 18 iterative ones), that hybrid CNN-attention architectures are gaining ground, and that research remains heavily concentrated on X-ray-to-CT registration. We conclude by identifying the absence of per-case uncertainty estimation and the strong neglect of temporal or sequential modelling as the two methodological gaps most consequential for clinical readiness, and discuss state-space models as a way to add temporal memory within intraoperative latency budgets. Further opportunities lie in more principled domain adaptation and in the integration of foundation models for representation learning.

title: Contrastive local learning in large nonlinear analog circuits
comment: 19 pages (13 main, 6 supplementary) and 11 figures (5 main, 6 supplementary)
summary: Machine learning in physical hardware promises to reduce training cost by colocating computation, memory and adaptation within device physics. Contrastive local learning networks (CLLNs) offer a compelling route: an electrical circuit relaxes to equilibrium in free and weakly clamped states, and each adaptive element updates from local voltage contrasts rather than backpropagated error signals. Yet whether nonlinear transistor implementations can scale beyond proof-of-concept circuits, and what design principles control that scaling, have remained unknown. Here we show that nonlinear analog circuits trained by contrastive local rules can learn larger machine-learning tasks and remain robust under hardware nonidealities. Using device-level circuit simulations, we systematically explore initialization, operating regime, loss-dependent clamping and training parameters, and scale CLLNs beyond ten thousand adaptive edges. The same local rule trains classifiers that reach the accuracy regime of conventional digital methods on Ionosphere and handwritten-digit benchmarks, and a network that autoregressively generates language over a 122-token vocabulary. These results establish the feasibility of local learning in large nonlinear analog circuits.

title: Uncertainty evaluation of length measurement by spectral domain interferometry with super-Gaussian windowing
summary: In this study, we evaluate the measurement uncertainty of spectral domain interferometry with super-Gaussian windowing, which has significant potential for interferometer-based dimensional calibration services owing to its simple configuration and nanometer-level precision. A super-luminescent diode (SLD) with a broadband spectrum was used as the light source for high-precision length measurement, and a frequency-calibrated spectrometer captured the spectral interference signal. The length measurement results were compared with a laser displacement interferometer. To evaluate the measurement uncertainty, numerical simulations were performed by considering the intensity-noise level of the CCD in the spectrometer and the frequency-axis uncertainty of the spectrometer. Through a comprehensive uncertainty analysis supported by numerical simulations, the combined standard uncertainty of the measured length was evaluated as sqrt((10 nm)^2 + (9.7x10^(-6)xL)^2). The resulting uncertainty budget provides a metrological basis for extending SLD-based SDI with super-Gaussian windowing toward interferometric dimensional calibration tasks over the millimeter-scale range.

title: Curvature-Aware Edge Dynamic GNNs for Low-$p_T$ Track Reconstruction at HL-LHC
summary: Particle track reconstruction in high-energy collider experiments is a computationally demanding combinatorial problem, traditionally solved by Kalman filters that scale poorly with increasing detector occupancy. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have recently emerged as a promising alternative. In this work, we introduce the Manifold Helical-IN, a novel Interaction Network architecture that explicitly embeds detector spacepoints onto a helical manifold chart using curvature-aware features. This geometric projection mathematically unrolls the tightly curling trajectories of low-momentum particles. Consequently, the network can distinguish true physical tracks from combinatorial noise with good precision. Evaluated on the TrackML challenge dataset, the proposed Manifold Helical-IN achieves a reconstruction efficiency of 0.9675 in the experimentally critical $p_T > 0.5$ GeV regime, approaching recently reported Transformer-based approaches. Crucially, the manifold embedding yields a fake track rate of 0.0037. This represents a 13-fold improvement over the baseline Helical-IN (0.0508). Furthermore, the model maintains good track coherence, as quantified by our proposed Mean Hit Recovery Fraction (MHRF) of 0.858, and achieves a highly efficient inference latency of approximately 150 ms per event on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU. These results represent a critical step toward real-time soft particle tracking for the High-Level Trigger (HLT). By operating within practical HLT latency budgets, this geometry-aware approach provides a pathway to recover soft, anomalous Beyond Standard Model signatures such as unclustered energy patterns (SUEPs), that routinely evade standard hardware filters.

title: A Tumour-Aware Multimodal Framework for Explainable Prediction of IDH Mutation in Gliomas from Multi-Sequence MRI
comment: 45 pages, 12 figures, 4 tables. Preprint of an article submitted for consideration in International Journal of Information Technology & Decision Making (World Scientific)
summary: Accurate prediction of isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH) mutation status is essential for glioma diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment planning. Although recent deep learning approaches have demonstrated promising performance, many rely on whole-brain feature extraction and provide limited interpretability. This study proposes a tumour-aware multimodal framework for explainable, non-invasive prediction of IDH mutation status from multiparametric magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). The proposed framework integrates four MRI sequences (T1, T1CE, T2, and FLAIR), tumour subregion segmentation, quantitative radiomic descriptors, and clinical information within a unified deep learning architecture. An ablation study was conducted to evaluate the contribution of tumour-aware learning, radiomic features, and clinical variables. Model performance was assessed using multiple complementary evaluation metrics, including accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, balanced accuracy, receiver operating characteristic analysis, confusion matrix evaluation, and Grad-CAM visualisation. Experimental results demonstrated that the proposed multimodal framework consistently outperformed the baseline MRI-only model, with the Clinical Fusion model achieving the strongest overall predictive performance. The integration of tumour-aware learning, radiomic descriptors, and clinical information progressively improved classification performance, while Grad-CAM visualisations indicated that the model predominantly focused on biologically relevant tumour regions. These findings suggest that tumour-aware multimodal feature integration enables accurate, interpretable, and non-invasive molecular profiling of gliomas and provides a promising foundation for future clinical decision support in precision neuro-oncology.

title: A charge-dependent electron emission yield from electron irradiated dielectrics
summary: The total electron emission yield (TEEY) of dielectric surfaces may vary during electron irradiation owing to charge accumulation within the material. In the present work, the generation, transport, and escape formulation of Dionne is extended by introducing an additional attenuation of secondary electrons that depends on trapped positive charge. The resulting emission law is coupled to a charge-balance equation, allowing the TEEY to be calculated as a function of incident energy and injected charge. The model is examined using measurements on polycrystalline Al2O3, from which effective cross sections describing interactions between trapped charge and secondary electrons are determined. Their mean value is then used to predict the evolution of the TEEY curves without further adjustment. Finally, an analytical approximation of the nonlinear charging law is derived to facilitate the implementation in electron-irradiation simulations.

title: Polarization Lifetime as a Design Axis for Task-Adaptive Photonic Reservoir Computing
summary: Photonic time-delayed reservoir computing (TDRC) based on conventional Class B lasers is limited by fragile external cavity mode (ECM) locking dynamics. Here, we show that engineering the polarization lifetime (T$_2$) with the carrier lifetime ($T$) reshapes the topology and stability of TDRC. Comparing four laser classes (Class A, Class B, Class C$_A$, and Class C$_B$), a finite polarization lifetime acts as an intrinsic dynamic filter, dissolving discrete ECM chaos grids into continuous, phase-tolerant operational basins. Information processing capacity (IPC) decomposition further exposes distinct computational profiles: matched Class C$_A$ achieves the highest nonlinear capacity (16.28) and the highest total capacity (19.29), whereas Class A exhibits the highest linear capacity (4.70). A task-dependent reversal governs hardware design: Class A and Class C$_A$ achieve comparable, and the lowest, NRMSE on short-horizon Mackey--Glass prediction (0.0103 and 0.0105, within one standard deviation), while the time-scale-matched Class C$_A$ dominates the higher-dimensional Lorenz (0.0506) and the experimental Santa Fe (0.4251) tasks. Linear-IPC ranking matches Mackey-Glass accuracy; nonlinear-IPC ranking matches the Lorenz exactly and Santa Fe within the mask-to-mask uncertainty. Under realistic quantum noise, resilience is dictated mainly by $T$, not T$_2$: Class A retains the lowest NRMSE (0.47) even at spontaneous emission factor $β$ = $10^{-1}$, whereas the long-carrier Class B degrades (0.98). A residual T$_2$-mediated benefit of 20$\%$ persists in the slow-carrier Class C$_B$ (0.78 vs. 0.98). Time-scale engineering thus offers a nuanced design paradigm for optical computing, where optimal hardware is set by the task's time-scale hierarchy rather than a universal figure of merit.

title: Rank-One Ultralight Dark Matter Response in a Full-Tensor Gravity Gradiometer
summary: A full-tensor superconducting gravity gradiometer whose four test masses carry two compositions in a $2+2$ pattern acquires a composition-dependent channel for dilaton-coupled ultralight dark matter. The reconstructed response is the rank-one tensor $\K=\gv_φ(t)\otimes\qv$, with the axis of $\qv$ fixed in advance by the material assignment, and obeys the parameter-free null condition $\K(\mathbf{I}-\Pq)=0$, which no gravity gradient or platform rotation alone can satisfy; it vanishes for a single composition. For copper and lead, the sensitivity reaches $d_{\hat m}-d_g\simeq3.4\times10^{-8}$, and $4.9\times10^{-10}$ with upgraded accelerometers.

title: X-Strata: Separating Aneurysms and Overlapping Vessels into Layers from 2D X-ray Angiography
comment: 22 pages, including 10 pages of supplementary material
summary: An X-ray angiogram sums every structure along a ray into one pixel. When vessels cross an aneurysm, they obscure part of it and mix their contrast into its filling curve. We present X-Strata, a network that separates a cine angiogram into three layers: the complete aneurysm sac, the vessels in front of it, and the vessels behind it. Contrast timing indicates how much each layer contributes to a pixel, and parallax between two views indicates their order, which a single view cannot determine. X-Strata first estimates the layers and their contrast curves, then uses the second view to assign vessels to the front or back layer, and lifts all layers into 3D. It learns from layer labels projected from same-session 3D rotational angiography, but needs only 2D cine runs and their acquisition geometry at inference. On 220 held-out patients from three centers (122 external), two-view X-Strata ranks first among 14 baselines, including VGGT and C$^2$RV, in recovering the sac where vessels overlap it (Dice 0.693 internal, 0.641 external) and in ordering the layers (balanced accuracy 0.703, 0.659). Its order accuracy exceeds that of all 11 end-to-end baselines by at least 4.1 points internally and 3.3 externally (Holm-adjusted $p < 0.001$) and grows with view separation. Recovered 3D sac surfaces have a median Chamfer distance of 0.34 mm on the internal cohort. X-Strata may therefore provide layered aneurysm and vessel information, including 3D sac shape, for patients who undergo only 2D angiography.

title: Blind in-memory arithmetic with confined skyrmions: doubling and successor functions on a skyrmion byte
summary: We present a skyrmionic-based computation platform, able to perform fully in-memory computing by collectively manipulating the skyrmions that serve as bits of the binary memory. The computation protocols are implemented through driving currents and adequately located anisotropy defects that modify the dynamics of the skyrmions along a magnetic track. Simulations demonstrating the feasibility of such an in-memory computing system are shown for several basic and simple mathematical operations with natural numbers, such as doubling and adding one (the successor function). We also discuss how further optimization of the geometry, barrier profiles, current amplitudes, and timing parameters could improve both the robustness and the overall practical feasibility of the system.

title: Antihelical Edge States in Photonic Metacrystals
summary: Antihelical edge states represent a gapless form of boundary transport in which modes with opposite spin counterpropagate along a given boundary, while modes sharing the same spin propagate in the same direction on opposite boundaries. Here we show that such states arise naturally within a modified Kane-Mele framework realized in an electromagnetic-dual photonic metacrystal with staggered bianisotropy. Reversing the spin-dependent next-nearest-neighbor coupling on one sublattice reorganizes the bulk spectrum into a spin-polarized Dirac semimetal characterized by spin-dependent energy shifts of the Dirac cones rather than a bulk gap. This bulk reorganization generates tilted edge-mode dispersions in zigzag ribbons and gives rise to antihelical edge transport coexisting with bulk states. Full-wave simulations confirm the corresponding bulk and edge behaviors. Extending the analysis to finite geometries, simulations further reveal discrete corner-localized modes. A realistic design based on split-ring metaatoms is proposed to realize the required staggered bianisotropy and spin-dependent energy shifts of the Dirac cones. Furthermore, we show that the tensorial freedom of the bianisotropic constitutive relations enables continuous manipulation of the electromagnetic pseudospin basis while preserving the antihelical boundary transport. These results provide a practical route for engineering unconventional gapless boundary transport in photonic Dirac systems.

title: Composition-dependent ultralight dark matter detection with a tetrahedral superconducting gravity gradiometer
summary: Tetrahedral superconducting gravity gradiometers designed as full-tensor gravitational-wave detectors, such as the ground-based mSOGRO design and the proposed lunar LANGO observatory, reconstruct the acceleration-gradient tensor from four test masses. We show that giving the four test masses two compositions in a $2+2$ arrangement adds a composition-dependent ultralight dark matter (ULDM) channel to that same tensor readout, with no separate dark-matter sensor and no dark-matter-specific readout. A coherently oscillating scalar accelerates each mass in proportion to its dilaton charge, and the tensor reconstruction leaves the charges only in a mean, rejected with the common mode, and a single vector $\qv$ proportional to the charge contrast $Δ\abaralpha_{AB}$ between the two materials. The response is the rank-one tensor $\K_{\ULDM}(t)=\gv_φ(t)\otimes\qv$, whose amplitude is set by the halo, independent of $m_φ$. The axis of $\qv$ is fixed in advance by the material assignment, so the response obeys the null condition $\K_{\ULDM}(\mathbf{I}-\Pq)=0$ at every instant, for any $\gv_φ$ including a virialized field with a stochastic gradient---an exact tensor discriminator against gravitational-wave signals; for a single composition $\qv=0$. With the gravitational-wave noise model, the coupling sensitivity for copper and lead test masses reaches $d_{\hat m}-d_g\simeq3.4\times10^{-8}$ for the baseline instrument and $4.9\times10^{-10}$ with upgraded accelerometers. The rank-one factorization and the null condition are summarized in a companion Letter; the present paper gives the derivations and the detector-level analysis.

title: Few-Shot Open-Set Hyperspectral Pixel-Wise Classification with Spatial Aware Label Propagation
summary: Pixelwise classification of hyperspectral images (HSI) is a fundamental task in remote sensing, but its deployment in real-world applications is often limited by the scarcity of labeled data and the presence of unknown classes at inference time. In this work, we propose Few-shot Open-set hyperspectral recognition from Self-Supervised Learning training (FOSSeL), a unified framework for few-shot, open-set hyperspectral pixelwise classification that does not require supervised training. The proposed approach first leverages self-supervised learning to construct a discriminative feature space from unlabeled data. Then, given a small set of labeled seed pixels, class predictions are obtained through spatially-aware graph-based label propagation over superpixel representations, enabling the joint exploitation of spectral similarity and spatial consistency. To address the open-set scenario, we introduce simple yet effective strategies to identify pixels that do not belong to the known classes. We evaluate FOSSeL on three benchmark hyperspectral datasets under multiple few-shot settings. The results show that the proposed framework achieves competitive or superior performance compared to fully supervised methods while maintaining robustness in the presence of unknown classes. These findings highlight the potential of combining self-supervised feature learning with graph-based inference for practical HSI analysis in low-annotation and open-world scenarios.

title: Design and Experimental Evaluation of a Low-Cost Immersion Cooling System
comment: 20 pages, 12 figures, 3 tables. CAD files: https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/SWZV7 ; firmware and data: https://github.com/koc003/Design-and-Experimental-Evaluation-of-a-Low-Cost-Immersion-Cooling-System-ESP32
summary: This paper presents a low-cost, open-source, single-phase immersion cooling testbed for studying liquid cooling of data center hardware. A 500 W titanium heater, standing in for server load, is submerged in a glass tank of mineral oil, a dielectric fluid. The heated oil is circulated by a magnetic drive pump through an air-cooled radiator. An ESP32 microcontroller logs three DS18B20 temperature sensors (heater surface, bulk fluid and ambient) and switches the pump, fan and heater through a relay module. The complete system costs INR 35,318 (about USD 380), built entirely from components available in India. At quasi-steady state under the full 500 W load, the heater surface reached 118.3 °C while the bulk oil stayed at 29.3 °C, only 8.0 °C above ambient. Thermal-resistance analysis shows that the heater-to-oil interface, limited by natural convection, accounts for about 92% of the total resistance (178.0 vs 16.0 m°C/W). The external loop therefore has spare capacity. CAD files, firmware and data are openly available, so the setup can be reproduced and used to compare dielectric fluids, loads and flow arrangements.

title: A Necessary and Sufficient Condition for Complete TE/TM Separability in Fully Anisotropic Waveguides
summary: A necessary and sufficient condition is established for complete transverse-electric/transverse-magnetic (TE/TM) separability in waveguides homogeneously filled with a fully anisotropic and lossless medium. The permittivity and permeability tensors are Hermitian positive-definite and may contain nonzero transverse--longitudinal coupling terms. Complete TE/TM separation occurs if and only if the transverse permeability block is proportional to the transpose of the transverse permittivity block and the corresponding transverse--longitudinal coupling vectors satisfy the same proportionality relation after complex conjugation. The longitudinal constitutive entries remain independent apart from positive definiteness. The condition is derived directly from the source-free Maxwell equations, and independent analyses of the TE and TM modes lead to the same material relation. Since no boundary condition enters the derivation, the criterion is independent of the boundary type. Full-vector waveguide mode analyses using our in-house programs for perfect-electric-conductor and Bloch-periodic waveguides, with material tensors satisfying and violating the condition, agree with the theoretical results.

title: Artificial Intelligence for VAMOS++: From Data Analysis to Intelligent Instrumentation
summary: The increasing complexity of nuclear-physics experiments calls for analysis methods that combine precision, efficiency, and reproducibility. This article reviews the integration of artificial intelligence into the analysis framework of the VAMOS++ large-acceptance magnetic spectrometer at GANIL and discusses its evolution toward intelligent instrumentation. Deep neural networks exploit nonlinear correlations between detector observables to reconstruct ion trajectories and identify atomic charge states and atomic numbers. These approaches achieve performance comparable to or better than conventional methods while substantially reducing manual intervention and processing time. Trajectory reconstruction reaches processing rates of millions of events per second, while particle identification using fractionally labelled events reduces analysis procedures from months or years to minutes. These advances support high-resolution isotopic identification and facilitate consistent analysis across experimental campaigns, benefiting nuclear structure, reaction dynamics, and fission studies. Ongoing developments extend this framework to detector self-calibration, using experimental data and physical constraints to determine detector responses with reduced reliance on dedicated calibration measurements or labelled reference datasets. Applications to segmented ionization chambers and tracking detectors illustrate the potential for integrating calibration, reconstruction, and performance monitoring. Together, these developments outline a path toward adaptive, self-optimizing instrumentation that can respond to changing experimental conditions and increase the scientific return of complex nuclear-physics experiments.

title: BeST: Beta splatted tomography for direct reconstruction from coherent imaging measurements
summary: Conventional coherent X-ray tomography requires the phase of each projection to be reconstructed with high fidelity. However, individual reconstructed projections might be flawed, e.g. due to positioning errors, yielding inconsistent tomographic reconstructions. By directly coupling phase retrieval and tomography, consistency is enforced through a common object volume. But reconstructing a full volume demands substantial computational resources. To reduce this demand, we introduce Beta Splatted Tomography (BeST), which represents the common object volume using compactly supported beta primitives with closed-form analytical projections, enabling efficient reconstruction directly from coherent scattering images. This representation substantially reduces the number of optimizable parameters compared to a voxel grid. We demonstrate BeST on experimental datasets from hard X-ray near-field holography and far-field ptychography measurements. In both cases, the joint technique improves reconstruction quality compared to two-step methods.

title: A trap-based platform for cooling and laser spectroscopy of fast ions toward radioactive-ion applications
summary: We report on the first experiments with the Stopping and Trapping of Radioactive Isotopes for Precision Experiments (STRIPE) segmented linear Paul trap. The intent for this apparatus is to serve as an efficient capture and laser-cooling trap for radioactive isotopes produced at radioactive ion beam facilities. We demonstrate the deceleration of 10 keV ion beams and their trapping and laser cooling into Coulomb crystals. As an initial spectroscopic benchmark, the dipole-forbidden $5s$ $^2S_{1/2}$ $\rightarrow$ $4d$ $^2D_{5/2}$ transition in $^{88}$Sr$^+$ was driven, partially resolving the Zeeman structure and yielding a Gaussian linewidth of 14.5(8) MHz, with the residual width attributed to the ions' micromotion. The lifetime of the metastable $4d$ $^2D_{5/2}$ state was measured to be 0.325(5)$_{\mathrm{stat}}$(4)$_{\mathrm{sys}}$ s, uncorrected for collisional quenching. Several measurements to quantify the cooling timescale, the detection rate of the photon collection region and the trap storage lifetime were also performed. The developed technique will allow radioactive ion beams to be decelerated and cooled for precision spectroscopy measurements.

title: Spectral dependence of Berry phase and topological bound states in the continuum in Möbius resonators
comment: Main text: 16 pages, 6 figures; Supplementary: 13 pages 7 figures
summary: The Möbius strip and the bulk Möbius resonator are of great interest to specialists in optics, acoustics, and quantum physics. Despite the apparent simplicity of the object and numerous publications, the Möbius resonator, like a magic box, still holds many surprises. Here, we demonstrate experimentally, theoretically and with a simple illustrative example that in a "thin" Möbius resonator with an odd number of twists, the longitudinal wavenumber is determined by the additional phase shift π (traditionally called the geometrical Berry phase) only if the total transverse index of the photonic mode is odd. For an even index, the Berry phase is zero. We also discovered "topological" quasi-bound states in the continuum in Möbius resonators with a square cross-section; they differ from "ordinary" ones by the exchange of azimuthal indices of the interfering modes in the anti-crossing region. Finally, we demonstrate an example of resonant topology by determining the dependence of the Berry phase on the Möbius resonator geometry based on the frequency difference between the eigenmodes of planar ring resonators and those of Möbius resonators. The discovered effects significantly expand our knowledge of the topology of single resonators and promise new practical applications.

title: Performance and Stability Studies of GEM Detectors for High Energy Physics Applications
summary: R\&D on different gas-filled detectors such as Gas Electron Multipliers (GEMs), Resistive Plate Chambers (RPCs) and straw tubes has been carried out in the detector laboratory of Bose Institute for more than a decade, keeping in mind present and future high-energy physics experiments. In this article, performance studies of a single-mask triple-GEM detector using a $^{55}$Fe X-ray source with an Ar/CO$_2$ (70/30) gas mixture are described. The study focuses mainly on the gain, energy resolution, count rate, and stability of the chamber under long-term irradiation. The experimental setup, methodology, and analysis results are presented.

title: D2ToF: One-Step Diffusion for Depth Super-Resolution from Lightweight Single-Photon LiDAR Waveforms
summary: Single-photon LiDAR (SPL) sensors offer exceptional temporal resolution and single-photon sensitivity for depth imaging. However, cost-effective SPL arrays typically suffer from extremely low spatial resolutions (e.g. $8\times 8$ pixels), limiting their real-world utility. In this paper, we propose a novel, one-step super-resolution framework, D2ToF, Distilled Diffusion for Time-of-Flight, that bridges the gap between high-fidelity generative modeling and real-time execution. Our approach uses an amortized variational distillation strategy that allows for a measurement-based data consistency term to be incorporated directly into the one-step training objective. This encourages that the synthesized high-resolution depth maps are consistent with the captured low-resolution Time-of-Flight (ToF) histograms. To overcome the severe ill-posedness of upsampling extremely degraded inputs, we introduce a multimodal guidance strategy. By leveraging a foundational monocular depth model to extract structural priors from a high-resolution reflectivity image, our network is guided by a rich triad of the ToF histogram, reflectivity map, and relative depth estimate. Experimental results outperform evaluated baselines, achieving $16\times$ spatial super-resolution (from $8\times 8 \times 100$ histograms to $128\times 128$ depth maps) at an accelerated inference speed of approximately $83$ milliseconds.

title: An Inverse-Designed Multilayer Selective Emitter for High-Efficiency Thermophotovoltaics
summary: High thermophotovoltaic (TPV) conversion efficiencies have typically relied on photovoltaic cells that reflect sub-bandgap radiation back toward the emitter. Here, we numerically investigate an alternative approach in which spectral selectivity is engineered primarily on the emitter side. We optimize an emitter consisting of 16-layer aperiodic MgO/Si coating on tungsten, for coupling to a GaSb cell with an antireflection coating and an Au mirror. A detailed-balance framework incorporates polarization- and angle-resolved emissivity, multiple reflections, and Auger nonradiative recombination. At an emitter temperature of 1500 K, the optimized structure suppresses 97.1% of the incident-blackbody-equivalent sub-bandgap power at the source; a further 1.9% is returned to the emitter by the cell, leaving 1.0% absorbed parasitically in the cell. The resulting modeled radiative-to-electrical conversion efficiency reaches 47.0%, compared with 30.8% for a SiC emitter paired with the same cell, while maintaining a comparable maximum electrical power density. These findings indicate that emitter-side spectral engineering could substantially relax cell-side photon-recycling requirements and provide significant improvement in TPV conversion.

title: Symmerty-Engineered Moire Metasurface for Multibeam Control
summary: Moiré metasurfaces offer a versatile platform for wavefront engineering through the relative rotation of periodic structures. Despite extensive demonstrations of continuous beam steering, the physical mechanisms governing beam multiplicity remain poorly understood, hindering the systematic design of multibeam radiation states. Here, we establish a predictive framework for engineering beam multiplicity in reflective moiré metasurfaces based on the dominant Fourier coefficients of their constituent patterns. We reveal that the rotational symmetry of these Fourier components in reciprocal space fully determines the symmetry of the resulting moiré unit cell and, consequently, its radiation characteristics. By further incorporating their phase information, both beam multiplicity and steering trajectories can be accurately predicted. We demonstrate this approach using reflective moiré metasurfaces constructed from patterns with p6m, p3m1, and p4m plane-group symmetries, achieving one-, two-, three-, four-, and six-beam radiation states with continuously tunable steering trajectories. Beyond symmetry-based design, we identify two additional degrees of freedom for beam multiplicity control. Selecting different rotation centers reshapes the phase distributions of the dominant Fourier coefficients, enabling further manipulation of beam multiplicity and spatial arrangement, while varying the relative twist angle alters the pairing of Fourier components, inducing transitions between distinct beam multiplicities. These findings establish a systematic framework for versatile and reconfigurable multibeam wavefront engineering.

title: Topology-based fast neutron background suppression and sterile-neutrino sensitivity in a segmented reactor ${\overlineν}_{e}$ detector
summary: Reactor electron antineutrinos are commonly detected through the inverse beta decay interaction, with a prompt positron followed by delayed neutron capture. In shallow or above-ground segmented organic scintillator detectors, correlated fast neutrons are a dominant background because proton recoils can mimic the prompt IBD signal. We study topology-based machine learning using the Indian Scintillator Matrix for Reactor Anti-Neutrinos detector as a case study. A multilayer perceptron is trained on reconstructed topological observables from detailed Geant4 simulations. The $\mathrm{F_{1}}$ score and bootstrap resampling on an independent validation sample yield a fixed threshold of $P{\mathrm{IBD}}>0.40$. Applied without further optimization to an independent testing sample, the MLP retains $\mathrm{(83.4\pm 0.7)\%}$ of IBD events and rejects $\mathrm{(77.3\pm 0.7)\%}$ of fast neutron events. In a controlled spectral benchmark using an independent AmBe fast neutron spectrum, the selection reduces the net candidate-spectrum deformation by $\mathrm{84\%}$. The energy dependent signal acceptance and residual fast neutron component are subsequently incorporated into a binned likelihood, which recovers the injected IBD signal strength as $\mathrm{\hatα=0.993^{+0.053}_{-0.048}}$, with an empirical goodness-of-fit probability of $0.434$. The expected sterile-neutrino sensitivity for the ISMRAN detector is evaluated at baselines of 13 m and 18 m, with two years of exposure at each baseline. For the nominal pre-MLP $S/B=1:2$ benchmark and the background model, retaining the classifier score in a joint ($\mathrm{E_{prompt}\times P_{IBD}}$) likelihood improves the 95\% C.L. sensitivity to $\sin^{2}2θ_{14}$ by a logarithmically averaged 7.9\% over $0.1\leqΔm_{41}^{2}\leq1~\mathrm{eV}^{2}$ relative to an energy-only likelihood with the same fast neutron contamination.

title: DecompJSCC: Joint Source-Channel Coding With Decoupled SNR and Rate Adaptation
comment: 5 pages,5 figures,1 table. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Vehicular Technology
summary: Deep joint source-channel coding (DeepJSCC) for image transmission must adapt to changes in the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and available transmission resources. However, some existing joint-adaptive methods condition the encoder on the requested rate, while others apply static masks after encoding. The former couples latent formation to the rate request, whereas the latter cannot adapt channel selection to image content. To address these limitations, we propose DecompJSCC, which decomposes joint adaptation into SNR-conditioned latent formation and post-encoding rate control within a single model. The encoder applies SNR-conditioned block attention residuals across all stages, aggregating intra-stage and cross-stage semantic representations. At the receiver, an adapter performs SNR-conditioned affine correction. We introduce a post-encoding rate-adaptive channel semantic budgeting (RCSB) module whose shared gate selects channels of the formed latent by image content, adjusts their gains, and keeps exactly the requested count. This keeps the encoder output independent of the rate request for a fixed image and SNR. Experimental results show that DecompJSCC outperforms SwinJSCC and SA-RA-JSCC in peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) across a range of SNR and rate settings, by 0.64 and 1.00 dB over SwinJSCC and by 0.97 and 0.96 dB over SA-RA-JSCC on Kodak and CLIC2021, while using only 7.5% of SwinJSCC's Adaptive ModNet parameters.

title: Optical Representation Neural Networks Enabled by Weakly Supervised Learning
summary: Diffractive optical neural networks (ONNs) show remarkable promise in high-speed and energy-efficient optical computing. However, most existing ONNs are optimized to reproduce predefined output intensity distributions, with the desired optical responses explicitly specified before training. Here, we introduce optical representation neural networks (ORNNs) enabled by coarse-grained weak supervision. Using handwritten Devanagari, Arabic, and English characters as three semantic groups, a modified contrastive objective encourages samples from the same script to cluster into similar optical representations. Remarkably, ORNNs improve the classification accuracy by approximately 9% over conventional supervised ONNs, while requiring only around 18% of the training steps to reach a stable test accuracy of 84.5%. These features can be selectively interpreted using corresponding semantic decoders. Building on this concept, we further realized semantic optical encryption with electronic neural network (ENN) decryption using experimentally acquired representations from a single-layer diffractive network fabricated by two-photon polymerization lithography (TPL). Here, we combine information from different scripts into a mixed optical ciphertext that is then first optically classified before being decrypted with a matched ENN. This work broadens the training paradigm of ONNs by coupling upstream optical representation learning with downstream task-specific decoding, opening new avenues for optical information processing.

title: High-Transmission Cryogenic Fiber-Optic U-Bench Filter for Ultra-Low-Background Single-Photon Detection in Superconducting Devices
summary: We report on our progress in implementing a cryogenic fiber-optic U-bench hosting an ultra-narrow bandpass filter, designed to mitigate the dominant fiber-coupled 300 K black-body background observed for superconducting single-photon detectors. While U-benches can be routinely aligned at room temperature to achieve minor optical losses, cooling them down results in substantial misalignment due to thermal contraction of their components. To mitigate the resulting losses, we have integrated cryo-compatible piezo stepper motors to the U-bench, enabling its in situ realignment while cold. In particular, this allows us to shift the temperature dependent transmission window of the used filter by rotating it with respect to the beam axis. First results show that our U-bench filter reaches a transmission coefficient of 38% (4.2 dB loss) at 40 K temperature. We project that the U-bench filter can reduce the black-body background down to $10^{-8}$ Hz and $10^{-3}$ Hz ranges for 1064 nm and 1550 nm wavelengths, respectively. With the expected background rates and the herein reported transmission coefficient, applying the U-bench filter in series with a transition edge sensor shows great potential in increasing the sensitivity of dedicated rare-event searches. We project that the noise-equivalent power for 1550 nm wavelength could be reduced down to $10^{-20}$ W Hz$^{-1/2}$ range if intrinsic background sources can be sufficiently mitigated.

title: Tunable Hybridization of Whispering Gallery Modes in High-Index Photonic Molecules
summary: Photonic molecules formed by coupled dielectric microresonators provide a platform for controlling collective optical modes, yet the interplay between molecular topology, resonator detuning, and dielectric environment in determining their spectral response remains insufficiently quantified. Here, we systematically quantify the evolution of Whispering Gallery Mode (WGM) hybridization in high-index TiO$_2$ and perovskite coated TiO$_2$ microresonators with molecular topology, and establish the corresponding effective inter-cavity coupling using a combined numerical and analytical analysis. We further show that perovskite-shell incorporation provides a diameter and thickness-dependent modification of the effective coupling, producing a non-monotonic response rather than a uniform suppression of coupling. Despite the resulting closely spaced hybridized resonances in the high-index perovskite environment, the supermodes remain spectrally resolvable, with $Q$-factor of order \(10^3\) for representative modes. The observed spectral splitting is quantitatively related to the effective inter-cavity coupling strengths, revealing a non-monotonic coupling response to perovskite-shell incorporation that depends on resonator size and shell thickness. These results establish molecular topology and dielectric environment as distinct parameters for controlling WGM hybridization, inter-cavity coupling, and spectral response, providing a basis for the design of coupled resonator systems for applications in optical sensing, filtering, switching, and other resonant photonic devices.

title: Commercial AlGaAs diodes provide simplified feedback for adaptive femtosecond pulse compression
summary: Maintaining high peak power in ultrashort laser pulses is essential for efficient nonlinear interactions, particularly in multiphoton microscopy. Dispersion introduced by optical components broadens these pulses and degrades their peak power, thus motivating adaptive pulse compression guided by pulse-width-dependent feedback. However, the conventional second-harmonic generation feedback requires a nonlinear crystal, spectral filtering, and careful optical alignment. Here, we investigate commercially available AlGaAs laser and light-emitting diodes as alternative two-photon absorption feedback sensors. Their photocurrent exhibits a quadratic dependence on average optical power and inverse dependence on pulse duration, which is consistent with the analytical model predicting maximum response for the shortest, single-peaked pulse. Both devices generated a measurable photocurrent at sub-milliwatt average power levels and showed a weaker polarization dependence than second-harmonic-generation-based solution. All three feedback methods achieved comparable mean compressed pulse durations of 210-228 fs. These results demonstrate effective adaptive pulse compression with a substantially simpler feedback.

title: Energy resolving optical transition-edge sensor approaching fundamental limits
comment: 9 pages, 7 figures, and additional supplemental materials in appendix
summary: Transition-edge sensors (TES) have long held promise for exhibiting single-photon spectral resolution with near-unity detection efficiency, no read noise, and negligible dark counts. A TES detector capable of simultaneously achieving these traits could be revolutionary in fields including quantum computing, quantum sensing, biological imaging, and the detection of life on alien worlds by spectroscopy of exoplanet atmospheres. The applicability of optical TES detectors in these fields has been limited by energy resolution results that differ significantly from the theoretical expectations. We report significant enhancement of the single-photon energy resolution of tungsten (W) TESs by mitigation of athermal phonon loss during the photon-absorption energy down-conversion cascade. Implementing barriers to phonon loss dramatically increased the TES energy resolution (delta E). We achieve delta E of 34 meV - 61 meV, with resolving power (R = E/delta E) of 24 - 43, in a band spanning 1550 nm - 471 nm. All relevant electrical/thermal device parameters are explored in order to model theoretical limits to delta E imposed by noise, and provide an estimate of the athermal phonon trapping factor. Based on a simple model of electrical, thermal, and phonon escape noise sources, we estimate a phonon trapping factor approaching 90% for our best performing TES architecture. These results bring optical TES technology closer to theoretical predictions and to achieving the ambitious goals of photon-starved optical spectroscopy and fault-tolerant photonic quantum computing.

title: Enhanced Hyperspectral Nano-FTIR Imaging by Neural-Network-Based Processing of Multiple Signal Harmonics
summary: Nano-FTIR spectroscopy combines infrared spectroscopy with nanometer-scale spatial resolution and enables hyperspectral nanoimaging. However, quantitative measurements typically rely on higher-harmonic near-field signals, which are largely background-free but suffer from low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). Lower harmonics provide substantially higher SNR but contain significant background contributions that distort the near-field response and hinder quantitative analysis. Here, we introduce a cross-harmonic neural network (CHNN) that exploits the complementary information encoded in multiple harmonic channels to denoise third-harmonic hyperspectral data. Trained directly on experimental nano-FTIR datasets, the CHNN uses first- and second-harmonic spectra to improve the SNR of the third-harmonic response. Applied to a PMMA/PS polymer blend, it substantially reduces noise while preserving spectral features and nanoscale spatial contrast. Compared with conventional single-harmonic denoising using an autoencoder, the CHNN achieves superior noise suppression. These results demonstrate the potential of lower-harmonic signals for improving hyperspectral nano-FTIR imaging without increasing acquisition time.

title: Unsupervised Anomaly Detection in Measured Neutron Flux Profiles of the SAFARI-1 Research Reactor
comment: 33 pages, 26 figures, submitted to Annals of Nuclear Energy
summary: Knowledge of the neutron flux distribution is essential for safe and effective reactor utilisation. In the SAFARI-1 research reactor, a set of axial flux profiles are periodically measured by activating natural copper wires inserted along the height of the fuel or control assemblies and subsequently measuring their activity using a sodium iodide detector. Improper wire insertion can, however, result in profiles that do not accurately represent the actual neutron flux distribution. Building on previously identified potential indicators of improper wire insertion, an automated approach based on unsupervised learning was developed to detect anomalous axial flux measurements. The measured data were preprocessed using missing-value imputation, decay correction, and normalisation. High-order polynomial fitting was then applied to characterise the axial flux profiles and derive features describing their shape. The Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise (DBSCAN) algorithm was employed to group flux profiles into regular and abnormal clusters based on these features with results matching the known groups. In addition, Convolutional Autoencoders were developed and trained on flux profiles from central and peripheral core positions to identify deviations from the regular profiles through reconstruction error, achieving better performance in central assemblies than in peripheral assemblies. The developed framework is intended to provide feedback to reactor operation by identifying potential wire-insertion problems in the manual technique used for axial flux monitoring at SAFARI-1.

title: Tunable Hybridization of Whispering Gallery Modes in High-Index Photonic Molecules
summary: Photonic molecules formed by coupled dielectric microresonators provide a platform for controlling collective optical modes, yet the interplay between molecular topology, resonator detuning, and dielectric environment in determining their spectral response remains insufficiently quantified. title: Demonstrating CBM Capabilities through $Λ$ Reconstruction with mCBM
summary:
The Compressed Baryonic Matter (CBM) experiment at the upcoming Facility for Antiproton and Ion Research (FAIR) is a high-rate fixed-target experiment designed to investigate nuclear matter at extreme baryon densities in relativistic nucleus-nucleus collisions. To enable high-statistics measurements of rare probes, CBM is designed to operate at event rates up to 10 MHz. This necessitates the development of fast and radiation-tolerant detectors, self-triggered front-end electronics, a free-streaming data acquisition architecture, and real-time event reconstruction capabilities. Prototype versions and pre-series productions of the CBM detector systems have been deployed in the mini-CBM demonstrator setup mCBM - an experimental precursor comprising sub-components of all major CBM systems, installed at the SIS18 facility of GSI/FAIR within the FAIR Phase-0 program.
  In 2024, Ni+Ni collisions at a kinetic beam energy of 1.93 AGeV and an average interaction rate of about 500 kHz were successfully recorded. This dataset enables a detailed evaluation of the operational performance of the detector systems as well as the complete CBM data chain, while the reconstruction of $Λ$ baryons, which constitute a relatively rare signal within the limited geometrical acceptance of mCBM, serves as a natural benchmark. This paper presents the first results on $Λ$ baryon reconstruction with the mCBM experiment, demonstrating the functionality of the detector technologies and the data chain for the upcoming full-scale CBM experiment.

title: Hybrid Quantum-Classical Sequence Models for Sample-Efficient Energy Regression in Simulated Calorimeter Showers
summary: Energy reconstruction from electromagnetic calorimeter data underpins particle identification, event reconstruction and precision measurements in high-energy physics. Machine learning already performs well on this task, yet two questions remain open: how much the choice of data representation matters, and whether hybrid quantum-classical models add value in practice. We compare classical and quantum-enhanced models for incident positron energy reconstruction on the CaloGAN dataset, a public benchmark of 100,000 simulated electromagnetic shower events spanning 1 to 100 GeV. Eight architectures, namely SVR, ANN, CNN and LSTM together with their quantum counterparts, are trained on three calorimeter representations: engineered physical features, calorimeter images, and longitudinal shower sequences. Models that follow the longitudinal development of the shower reach the highest accuracy, which points to the value of physically informed representations. The hybrid QLSTM gives the lowest reconstruction error, with an RMSE of 0.294 GeV. Under matched-data conditions with only 1,500 training events, the QLSTM improves on the classical LSTM by 52.7% and also surpasses an LSTM trained on the full set. These observations indicate that longitudinal representations are central to calorimeter energy reconstruction and give preliminary evidence that hybrid quantum-classical sequence models can be more sample-efficient for regression in high-energy physics.

title: Waveform-based pulse timing enhanced by self-supervised neural regression models for digital nuclear instrumentation
summary: With the rapid development of high-sampling-rate digital nuclear devices, their applications in nuclear facilities and related fields become more acceptable, and will possibly become widespread due to the versatility and flexibility of waveform sampling systems. When digitizers reach hundreds of megahertz or gigahertz, their lower limit in time measurement probes into the sub-nanosecond region, expediting their use in a bunch of time-critical scenarios. While conventional algorithms coupled with digital sampling techniques realize fair pulse timing in certain conditions, the potentials are still open to compact and efficient machine learning models. In this paper, we intend to boost the performance of pulse timing with a new paradigm of self-supervised learning on matched waveform pairs. The proposed method combines the mainstream self-supervised loss and the auxiliary weakly-supervised loss on the reference set, jointly improving the timing performance. We apply the method in a gamma/neutron-mixed radiation field, common in nuclear facilities. The simulation and experimental results show that, the proposed method not only outperforms conventional timing algorithms, but also surpasses neural network models based on supervised learning alone. Considering the trained model is lightweight and computationally efficient, it is promising to deploy it on edge devices, like economical microcontrollers with neural processing units.

title: Design and Experimental Evaluation of a Low-Cost Immersion Cooling System
comment: 20 pages, 12 figures, 3 tables. CAD files: https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/SWZV7 ; firmware and data: https://github.com/koc003/Design-and-Experimental-Evaluation-of-a-Low-Cost-Immersion-Cooling-System-ESP32
summary: This paper presents a low-cost, open-source, single-phase immersion cooling testbed for studying liquid cooling of data center hardware. A 500 W titanium heater, standing in for server load, is submerged in a glass tank of mineral oil, a dielectric fluid. The heated oil is circulated by a magnetic drive pump through an air-cooled radiator. An ESP32 microcontroller logs three DS18B20 temperature sensors (heater surface, bulk fluid and ambient) and switches the pump, fan and heater through a relay module. The complete system costs INR 35,318 (about USD 380), built entirely from components available in India. At quasi-steady state under the full 500 W load, the heater surface reached 118.3 °C while the bulk oil stayed at 29.3 °C, only 8.0 °C above ambient. Thermal-resistance analysis shows that the heater-to-oil interface, limited by natural convection, accounts for about 92% of the total resistance (178.0 vs 16.0 m°C/W). The external loop therefore has spare capacity. CAD files, firmware and data are openly available, so the setup can be reproduced and used to compare dielectric fluids, loads and flow arrangements.

title: MR-ToF-assisted In-Source Resonance Ionization Spectroscopy at IGISOL
comment: ARIS2026 proceedings (from the 5th Conference on Advances in Radioactive Isotope Science, which took place in June 2026 in Fukushima, Japan)
summary: Multi-Reflection Time-of-Flight Mass Spectrometer (MR-ToF-MS) assisted in-source laser resonance ionization spectroscopy (RIS) has been implemented at the Ion Guide Isotope Separator On-Line (IGISOL) facility, University of Jyväskylä. Exotic nuclei, produced via fusion-evaporation reactions, are stopped and neutralized in a hot-cavity catcher, and selectively laser-ionized through a multi-step resonance ionization scheme before being transported to the MR-ToF-MS device. This combination of techniques is aimed at optically probing the very exotic N=Z nuclei in the immediate vicinity of $^{100}$Sn. The laser system, hot-cavity ion source, isobaric purification and detection stages are described. A representative hyperfine-structure spectrum of the proton-rich silver isotope $^{101}$Ag is presented as a case example.

title: MID: a muon detector for the ALICE 3 upgrade project
summary:
The success of the ALICE programme has allowed to study the hottest state of matter created in the laboratory: the strongly-interacting quark-gluon plasma (sQGP). However, some fundamental questions on the sQGP and other aspects of the strong interaction will remain open even after LHC Run 4. To address this, the ALICE collaboration has proposed a major upgrade of its detector, known as ALICE 3. Among the subdetectors considered for this upgrade is the muon identification detector (MID), whose aim is to contribute to the study of charmonium and exotic-hadron production in heavy-ion collisions. While the baseline design consists of plastic-scintillator-based chambers placed around a cylindrical magnetic iron absorber, different detector technologies are under evaluation for the MID, including multi-wire proportional chambers.
  This proceeding presents the results of two MID prototypes based on FNAL-NICADD scintillator bars, Kuraray fibers and Hamamatsu SiPMs, characterized in test beams at the CERN Proton Synchrotron with 3 GeV/$c$ muon- and pion-enriched beams. The muon efficiency as well as the hadron suppression obtained using machine learning techniques will be discussed.

title: Study of neutron flux redistribution and shadowing effect in rod worth measurements with the rod drop experiment
comment: 16 pages, 7 figures. Author manuscript based on the October 2023 version. The peer-reviewed article was published in Nuclear Engineering and Design 415 (2023), 112672. Please cite the published article as the version of record
summary: This study investigates neutron flux redistribution and the shadowing effect between control rods during rod-worth measurements using the rod-drop experiment. A simulation-based instrumental calibration methodology is proposed to account for spatial effects on neutron detector responses and improve the accuracy of reactivity measurements. The IPEN/MB-01 research reactor was modeled using the MCNP Monte Carlo neutron transport code. Reactivity behavior during the initial transient of the rod-drop experiment (t < 10 s) was evaluated and compared with experimental measurements using the source-jerk method. The methodology quantifies control rod shadowing and detector-dependent neutron flux redistribution, allowing correction factors to be established for the measured reactivity. Control-bank worth values obtained through the stable-period method were adopted as reference measurements. The reported maximum deviations from the reference values were 0.5% and 11.3%, respectively. The results demonstrate the relevance of spatial neutron flux effects, control rod interactions, and detector calibration in rod-drop experiments, providing a computational and experimental basis for improving control rod worth measurements in research reactors.

title: Observation of Non-Equilibrium Phonon Loss Across a Solid-Superfluid Interface
summary: We measure the performance of an athermal phonon calorimeter in vacuum and in thermal contact with superfluid $^4$He. Using a cryogenic photon calibration system, we show that the superfluid suppresses the collection of the phonon signal by over 99\%. We conclude that submerged sensors will not benefit TESSERACT's superfluid helium dark matter target, but that superfluid helium may be useful to superconducting qubits as a sink for athermal phonons generated by radiation and other spontaneous sources. Our measurement is the first probe of solid-to-superfluid phonon transmission at energies higher than those stably supportable by the superfluid. We discuss thermal flow inside the calorimeter, as well as systematics from an alternative calibration scheme.

title: Axis-selective AC magnetic-field imaging in the tens-of-megahertz regime using RF-dressed continuous-wave scanning NV magnetometry
summary: Spatially resolved magnetic-field imaging reveals material properties and local currents in microelectronic devices. Conventional pulsed scanning nitrogen-vacancy (NV) magnetometry (SNVM) faces increasingly stringent microwave (MW) pulse-control requirements for detecting radio-frequency (RF) magnetic fields at frequencies ranging from tens to hundreds of megahertz. To address this challenge, we implement an RF-dressed continuous-wave (CW) sensing scheme for SNVM and demonstrate AC magnetic-field imaging at 33.5 MHz. The method exploits electron-spin double resonance in the NV spin-1 three-level system: the target RF magnetic field coherently couples two spin eigenstates, forming RF-dressed states whose splittings are detected in continuous-wave electron-spin double resonance (CW-ESDR) spectra under continuous laser, MW, and RF excitation. This approach avoids short, high-power MW pulses and synchronization between the RF field and a pulsed sensing sequence. Using an NV-ensemble diamond probe integrated with an atomic force microscope (AFM), we image the Oersted field of an RF-driven L-shaped microcircuit. Successively selecting three crystallographic NV axes by static bias-field control yields maps of RF magnetic-field projection magnitudes, with distinct distributions qualitatively reproduced by Biot-Savart calculations. Transverse bias-field control also tunes the RF-coupled spin-state transition frequency from 14.4 to 89.3 MHz, as characterized by spectroscopy and Hamiltonian analysis, with RF-dressed resonances directly observed in CW-ESDR spectra at 89.3 MHz. Together with previous RF magnetic-field detection up to 632 MHz using the same RF-dressed CW sensing principle in a confocal NV setup, these results support extending AC magnetic-field imaging with SNVM toward the hundreds-of-megahertz regime and, with additional phase information, vector magnetic-field reconstruction.

title: A trap-based platform for cooling and laser spectroscopy of fast ions toward radioactive-ion applications
summary: We report on the first experiments with the Stopping and Trapping of Radioactive Isotopes for Precision Experiments (STRIPE) segmented linear Paul trap. The intent for this apparatus is to serve as an efficient capture and laser-cooling trap for radioactive isotopes produced at radioactive ion beam facilities. We demonstrate the deceleration of 10 keV ion beams and their trapping and laser cooling into Coulomb crystals. As an initial spectroscopic benchmark, the dipole-forbidden $5s$ $^2S_{1/2}$ $\rightarrow$ $4d$ $^2D_{5/2}$ transition in $^{88}$Sr$^+$ was driven, partially resolving the Zeeman structure and yielding a Gaussian linewidth of 14.5(8) MHz, with the residual width attributed to the ions' micromotion. The lifetime of the metastable $4d$ $^2D_{5/2}$ state was measured to be 0.325(5)$_{\mathrm{stat}}$(4)$_{\mathrm{sys}}$ s, uncorrected for collisional quenching. Several measurements to quantify the cooling timescale, the detection rate of the photon collection region and the trap storage lifetime were also performed. The developed technique will allow radioactive ion beams to be decelerated and cooled for precision spectroscopy measurements.

title: A Double Sided LGAD-Based Detector Providing Timing, Position, and Track Angle Information
comment: Posting to the archive of a study initially submitted as a Fermilab report in 2022. 10 pages, 5 figures
summary: We describe a detector concept which combines small pixels enabled by 3D sensor-electronics integration with gain produced by a Low Gain Avalanche Diode (LGAD) layer. The detector is double-sided, with electrons collected by the cathode, which provides timing information, and an anode with small pixels to provide position and angle information. The cathode can be coarse grained, providing timing with fewer fast amplifiers to limit power consumption. The anode layer benefits from the gain of the LGAD, with larger signals that also limit the power needed. Position can be reconstructed by measuring the pattern of total charge deposited on the anode. Angle and depth of charge deposit can be measured by the shapes of the anode pulses. We describe a possible assembly technology based on 3D integration.

title: Real-time Electron Tagging by Cyclotron Radiation Emission Spectroscopy in the PTOLEMY experiment
summary: The PTOLEMY project aims at measuring the neutrino mass and, in the future, the Cosmic Neutrino Background from Tritium endpoint measurement. The Radio-Frequency (RF) Tracker is a sub-detector with the goal of measuring in real time the electrons by exploiting the Cyclotron Radiation Emission Spectroscopy. In this work, an overview of the PTOLEMY project is given together with the design, simulation, construction and commissioning of the RF Tracker prototype: the Electron Trap. The measurements and data analysis of the Electron Trap are presented, establishing the primary path for the development of the RF Tracker.

title: Oversampled Filter Bank Channelizer for Cryogenic Detectors
summary: We present the field programmable gate array (FPGA) implementation of an oversampled gener- alized DFT (GDFT) filter bank, optimized for its usage in the readout of cryogenic detectors, such as the microwave kinetic inductance detectors (MKID). A polyphase structure is derived underlin- ing the efficiency of complex valued subband processing, raised by a GDFT modulation. For the latter, a fast Fourier algorithm realization may be used, yielding a highly efficient polyphase imple- mentation for arbitrary integer decimation ratios. The filter bank is tested through a 16-channel GDFT channelizer. The implementation is based on the Xilinx Zynq family of FPGAs and aims to show the data reuse and flexibility offered by the GDFT channelizer structure. General design criteria are summarized for the 16-channel polyphase filter bank channelizer. The performance in hardware resource usage is also presented, taking into account one of the main objetives of the current physics experiments, aiming to have extremely large readout format.

title: Uncertainty evaluation of length measurement by spectral domain interferometry with super-Gaussian windowing
summary: In this study, we evaluate the measurement uncertainty of spectral domain interferometry with super-Gaussian windowing, which has significant potential for interferometer-based dimensional calibration services owing to its simple configuration and nanometer-level precision. A super-luminescent diode (SLD) with a broadband spectrum was used as the light source for high-precision length measurement, and a frequency-calibrated spectrometer captured the spectral interference signal. The length measurement results were compared with a laser displacement interferometer. To evaluate the measurement uncertainty, numerical simulations were performed by considering the intensity-noise level of the CCD in the spectrometer and the frequency-axis uncertainty of the spectrometer. Through a comprehensive uncertainty analysis supported by numerical simulations, the combined standard uncertainty of the measured length was evaluated as sqrt((10 nm)^2 + (9.7x10^(-6)xL)^2). The resulting uncertainty budget provides a metrological basis for extending SLD-based SDI with super-Gaussian windowing toward interferometric dimensional calibration tasks over the millimeter-scale range.
